meta.title: Who really said "You can't cross the sea merely by standing and staring at the water"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to Rabindranath Tagore, but the line is in none of his verified works — its only documented source is a 1968 compilation published 27 years after his death.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You can't cross the sea merely by standing and staring at the water'?
meta.ogDescription: Widely pinned on Tagore, and consistent with his aphorisms — yet no primary work contains it. Earliest trace: N.B. Sen's 1968 compilation.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1861–1941 · Bengali poet & polymath; first non-European Nobel laureate in Literature
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Tagore and consistent with his aphoristic voice (compare Stray Birds §242, “This life is the crossing of a sea…”), but the exact line is in none of his verified works. Its earliest documented appearance is a 1968 secondary compilation that attributes it to him without citing any primary source.

source.heading: Where the line actually shows up

docMeta.dd: None verified — often filed loosely near Stray Birds, but not in it
Wit and Wisdom of Gandhi, Nehru, Tagore, comp. N. B. Sen (1968)
the compiler’s “Adventure” heading, no primary citation

source.excerpt: You can’t cross the sea merely by standing and staring at the water. Don’t let yourself indulge in vain wishes.
trail: The Wikiquote entry for Tagore lists the line but sources it only to the 1968 compilation — it is not one of the numbered Stray Birds aphorisms it sits near.
Tagore’s actual Stray Birds (1916) contains no such line; its nearest sea image is §242, “This life is the crossing of a sea, where we meet in the same narrow ship.”
The line’s only traceable home is N. B. Sen’s 1968 anthology, published 27 years after Tagore’s death, which attributes it to him with no source.
No Quote Investigator study exists, so the claim rests on that lone secondary anthology rather than any documented primary work.
source.excerptNote: As printed in N. B. Sen’s 1968 compilation, where the two sentences run together under “Adventure.” The compilation names Tagore but gives no book, speech, or date.

sourceLink.text: Wit and Wisdom of Gandhi, Nehru, Tagore (1968), full text at the Internet Archive

source.rightsNote: The exact wording cannot be tied to any identifiable Tagore work or first-publication date — its earliest documented appearance is a 1968 secondary compilation. Because the origin of the wording is unknown, no copyright or public-domain status can honestly be asserted.

author.name: Rabindranath Tagore
author.heading: About Rabindranath Tagore
author.metaLine: 1861–1941 · Bengali poet, essayist & composer; first non-European Nobel laureate in Literature (1913)
author.bio: Rabindranath Tagore reshaped Bengali literature and music and won the 1913 Nobel Prize in Literature, largely for his own English rendering of Gitanjali. He wrote thousands of poems, songs, plays, and aphorisms — including the terse Stray Birds collection — which makes him a natural, and unusually frequent, magnet for feel-good lines he never actually published.

misattribution.heading: How this one travels
misattribution.intro: The problem here isn’t a rival author — it’s false precision. The line is routinely presented as if it came from a specific Tagore book, when no such book has ever been shown to contain it.

items.scope: Attributed to a work that doesn’t contain it
items.why: Quote sites and even Wikiquote file the line beside the Stray Birds aphorisms, but a full read of Stray Birds (1916) turns up nothing of the kind — only §242’s unrelated “This life is the crossing of a sea.”

items.who: “From The King of the Dark Chamber”
items.why: Some search engines volunteer this play as the source, but the full text of the play contains no line about crossing the sea or staring at water.
The vast majority of appearances give only the name, tracing back to a chain of quote databases rather than to anything Tagore is documented to have written or said.

misattribution.truthLine: The furthest back the wording can be traced is N. B. Sen’s 1968 compilation — a posthumous secondary source that names Tagore but cites no work, so the exact wording remains credibly attributed rather than verified.

context.heading: Why the doubt matters
lead: Tagore is one of the internet’s busiest quotation magnets: an enormous, aphoristic body of work in two languages makes almost any tidy piece of wisdom feel plausibly his. That plausibility is exactly what lets unsourced lines stick.

This one may well trace to something Tagore actually said or wrote — the tone fits, and a 1968 anthologist thought so too. But ‘fits his style’ and ‘printed in a later collection’ are not the same as a located page, which is why the honest label here is attributed, not verified.
context.pull: Sounds like Tagore, filed under Tagore — but never yet found in Tagore.
